props.title: Across 110th Street
props.initialSlug: Cops hunt corrupt police in gritty Harlem crime saga

sections.content: Across 110th Street (1972) stands as one of the grittiest and most unflinching crime films of the 1970s, blazing a trail that later influenced Taxi Driver (1976) and The Warriors (1979). Director Barry Shear captured the raw desperation of Harlem's streets with a documentary-like intensity that put it leagues ahead of standard blaxploitation fare. While films like Shaft (1971) played up the cool factor, Across 110th Street dove deep into systemic corruption, racial tensions, and the brutal economics of survival. Yaphet Kotto and Anthony Quinn deliver powerhouse performances as cops navigating a powder keg after three small-time criminals steal from both the Italian mob and black gangsters.

sections.content: The film's unflinching violence and moral ambiguity marked a decisive shift from earlier crime pictures. While The French Connection (1971) showed police brutality in white neighborhoods, Across 110th Street exposed how corruption and violence plagued both law enforcement and criminals across racial lines. The film's influence echoes through later works like New Jack City (1991) and American Gangster (2007), which similarly explored the complex power dynamics between cops, criminals, and communities.

Bobby Womack's legendary title song, later featured prominently in Jackie Brown (1997), captures the film's raw emotional core. Like Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song (1971) and The Mack (1973), the music becomes inseparable from the film's gritty portrayal of urban life. Director Barry Shear and cinematographer Jack Priestley created a visual template for urban crime films that influenced everything from Mean Streets (1973) to Training Day (2001). sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond its era, visible in works like Dead Presidents (1995) and Brooklyn's Finest (2009). Its unflinching examination of racial politics and police corruption provided a template for modern crime dramas like The Wire (2002-2008) and Sicario (2015). The movie's realistic portrayal of cross-cultural criminal enterprises and law enforcement's compromised response feels remarkably contemporary.
